text: And the pattern under all of it is older than anyone now living it.
Paul Cornell bought these blocks in 1853 and sold the idea of a refined lakefront suburb, with wide lots and a fast train downtown.
The 1893 fair brought the crowds and the prestige.
The University of Chicago rose nearby in the 1890s, funded by John D.
Rockefeller, and it never stopped growing.

In the 1950s and 60s it backed the urban renewal that bulldozed swaths of Hyde Park and Kenwood and pushed thousands of families out, many of them Black families, all of it carried out in the name of saving the neighborhood.
Then in our own decade the university kept moving south across the Midway into Woodlawn, with new dorms and acquired property, the same direction the prices were rising.
Now the Obama Center sits at the edge of it all.
Each time, across a hundred and seventy years, the shape is the same.
A powerful institution arrives, the ground around it gains value, and the people already there are left to wonder whether the place they helped build still has room for them.
A hundred and seventy-three years after Cornell first walked these blocks, the question underneath this whole neighborhood, who this ground is really for, still isn't settled.
